To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dissemination of evidence-based psychological treatments for eating disorders is hindered by clinician attitudes and a lack of trained therapists.

the research-practice gap in eating disorder treatment is a serious concern, that the gap is not unique to eating disorders, that there are many barriers to the implementation of empirically supported treatment, that there is a growing body of research examining these barriers, and that there are promising developments to address the gap.

(1) despite the availability of evidence-based psychological treatments, the research-practice gap remains wide; (2) this gap is due in large part to clinician attitudes, the lack of sufficient trained providers, and the lack of scalable treatment delivery and training methods; and (3) recent efforts to expand treatment availability through the use of technology and training of lay providers have been promising.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dissemination and implementation (D&I) of evidence-based treatments for eating disorders.
how we can best use evidence-based treatments to improve outcomes for those with eating disorders.
the dissemination and implementation, rather than development of new treatments, although the latter is an area that has also received some attention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we know a lot about what works in terms of treatment for eating disorders, but that we know less about how best to disseminate and implement this knowledge in clinical practice.
there is insufficient evidence on which to make a definitive conclusion regarding the effectiveness of any particular dissemination strategy.
we know that evidence-based treatments work, but we don't know why so few people with eating disorders receive such treatments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are in a position to deliver evidence-based psychological treatments more widely and to more people.

there are promising approaches to disseminating evidence-based psychological treatments for eating disorders, but that there are still significant barriers to overcome before such treatments can be routinely available to the majority of those with eating disorders.
the evidence base for evidence-based treatments is strong, but there is still a long way to go to achieve the goal of widespread implementation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
while there are many barriers to implementing empirically supported treatments in eating disorders, there are also a number of strategies for overcoming these barriers.
while progress is being made, more needs to be done to ensure that evidence-based treatments are available to those in need.

the research-practice gap in eating disorder treatment can be addressed by developing scalable models of treatment delivery, and that such models are feasible, effective and acceptable to clinicians and patients.
